person.name: Frank_Lloyd_Wright
person.summary: Frank Lloyd Wright was an American architect whose long career reshaped modern architecture through the Prairie School, Usonian housing ideas, and major works such as Fallingwater and the Guggenheim Museum design. He also wrote widely and trained generations of apprentices through the Taliesin Fellowship.

chapters.headline: Wisconsin Beginnings
chapters.bridge_statement: In a restless household, an early certainty takes root—one that will demand a larger world.

chapters.headline: Forged in Chicago
chapters.bridge_statement: Opportunity turns ruthless in the big city, where ambition finds its first true discipline.

chapters.headline: Taliesin Reckoning
chapters.bridge_statement: A new voice rises from the prairie—then insists on a life bold enough to burn.

chapters.headline: Tokyo Monumental Gamble
chapters.bridge_statement: Far from home, scale and risk collide, testing whether vision can survive enormity.

chapters.headline: Desert Studio Revival
chapters.bridge_statement: When the commissions thin, he builds something harder to erase than a building: a way of living.

chapters.headline: Curves Against Time
chapters.bridge_statement: In old age, he wagers everything on form—daring the public to follow where space leads.

conclusion: Frank Lloyd Wright turned private conviction into public space, repeatedly remaking himself when scandal, loss, or fashion tried to end him. His buildingsand the Taliesin Fellowship behind themleft architecture more daring, more human, and permanently less obedient.

events.date_note: Wright sometimes claimed a birth year of 1869, but official records support 1867
events.title: Born in Richland Center, Wisconsin
events.description: Frank Lloyd Wright was born in Richland Center, Wisconsin, to William Cary Wright, a musician and occasional preacher, and Anna Lloyd Jones, a teacher from the close-knit Lloyd Jones family. In later years Wright liked to frame his childhood as a kind of early prophecy: a mother who nurtured ambition, a household that moved and strained, and a boy already collecting shapes and ideas that would become buildings.

events.title: Learns Froebel design blocks
events.description: As a child, Wright spent extensive time with [[Froebel gifts|Froebel kindergarten blocks]] purchased by his mother, Anna Lloyd Jones. He later credited these geometric exercises with shaping his lifelong sense of form, pattern, and spatial compositionthe kind of quiet training that made structure feel like play, and play feel like destiny.

Froebel gifts.explanation: A set of early-childhood educational toys devised by Friedrich Fröbel—geometric blocks and other materials used in kindergarten to teach form, pattern, and spatial relationships.

events.title: Family separation and divorce
events.description: Wrights parents separated as his adolescence began, amid financial strain and an unstable home life. The divorce was finalized in 1885, after which his father, William Cary Wright, left Wisconsin; Wright later said he never saw him again. The break became a private fault lineone he would revisit in his own restless patterns of attachment and escape.

events.title: Studies civil engineering
events.description: Wright enrolled at the [[University of WisconsinMadison|University of WisconsinMadison]] in 1886 as a special student to study civil engineering, but left without earning a degree. The decision was less a failure than a pivot: he chose the speed and severity of office work over the patience of classrooms, aiming straight for architectural practice through apprenticeship.

University of Wisconsin–Madison.explanation: The main campus of the University of Wisconsin system in Madison, a major U.S. public research university founded in 1848.

events.title: Moves to Chicago as a draftsman
events.description: In 1887, seeking opportunity in the booming building market, Wright moved to Chicago and looked for work in architectural offices. He was hired as a draftsman by Joseph Lyman Silsbee, where he gained early office experience on church and residential commissions and further refined his drafting and presentation skills.

events.title: Trains under Louis Sullivan
events.description: In 1888, Wright joined [[Adler & Sullivan|Adler & Sullivan]], working under Louis Sullivan and absorbing the firms modern approach to form and ornament. He rose to become head draftsman for residential work, gaining confidence and responsibilitywhile also taking on unauthorized side commissions that foreshadowed his eventual independence.

Adler & Sullivan.explanation: A Chicago architectural partnership (Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan) known for influential late-19th-century commercial buildings and for mentoring Frank Lloyd Wright early in his career.

events.title: Marries Catherine Tobin
events.description: In 1889, Wright married [[Catherine Tobin|Catherine Lee Kitty Tobin]], beginning a family life that ran alongside his rapid ascent in the Chicago area. The marriage would later become a public point of tension when he left home in 1909, and the private became inseparable from the professional.

Catherine Tobin.explanation: Wrights first wife, commonly called Kitty; their marriage and six children formed the domestic backdrop to his early career.

events.title: Establishes independent practice
events.description: After a rupture with [[Adler & Sullivan|Adler & Sullivan]] over his private commissions, Wright launched his own Chicago-area practice. He soon created a home-and-work base in Oak Park; by 1898, his studio there became a center for early innovations as he developed the language later associated with the [[Prairie School]] movement.

images.caption: Frank Lloyd Wright Home and Studio, Oak Park, Illinois

Adler & Sullivan.explanation: The Chicago architectural partnership of Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan (active 18811895), where Wright worked before starting his own practice.

Prairie School.explanation: A Midwestern architectural movement known for horizontal lines, open plans, and designs meant to harmonize with the landscape.

events.title: Leaves with Mamah Cheney
events.description: In 1909, Wright left his wife and children in Oak Park and traveled to Europe with Mamah Borthwick Cheney, a decision that triggered a major public scandal and damaged his standing in the United States. While abroad, he shaped a publication-ready record of his worklater known as the [[Wasmuth Portfolio]]that helped carry his designs to European audiences and future modernists.

images.caption: Frederick C. Robie House, Chicago, Illinois

Oak Park.explanation: A suburb immediately west of Chicago where Wright lived and maintained his home and studio at the time he left for Europe in 1909.

Wasmuth Portfolio.explanation: An influential early publication of Wrights designs that helped introduce his work to architects in Europe.

events.title: Builds Taliesin in Wisconsin
events.description: In 1911, Wright began building Taliesin near Spring Green, Wisconsin, as a personal refuge and working estate shaped by his relationship with Mamah Cheney. The compound became both a declaration of defiance and a laboratory: architecture tied to a specific landscape, daily life arranged as an extension of design, and a place he would return toeven after disasterto begin again.

events.title: Taliesin murders and fire
events.description: While Wright was away in Chicago on a project, a Taliesin staff member, [[Julian Carlton|a Barbadian-born servant employed at Taliesin]], set fire to the residence and murdered Mamah Borthwick Cheney, her two visiting children, and several others at the estate near Spring Green, Wisconsin. The catastrophe became one of the most notorious episodes of Wrights lifea moment of brutal rupture that left him devastated, yet determined to rebuild.

Julian Carlton.explanation: A Barbadian-born servant employed at Wright’s Taliesin who carried out the arson-and-axe attack on August 15, 1914; he later died after ingesting acid.

events.title: Designs Imperial Hotel Tokyo
events.description: Wright undertook the ambitious [[Imperial Hotel, Tokyo|Imperial Hotel project]] in Tokyo, one of his most important international commissions. The long, complex effort expanded his reach beyond the United States and demonstrated his ability to integrate structure, ornament, and planning at monumental scaleculminating in a building that opened in 1923.

Imperial Hotel, Tokyo.explanation: A major luxury hotel in Tokyo whose second main building (designed by Wright, commissioned in the 1910s and opened in 1923) became famous for its bold design and for surviving the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake.

events.title: Marries Olgivanna Lazović
events.description: Wright met Olgivanna Lazovi7 in November 1924, and after a turbulent interlude in his personal life, married her in 1928. The couple went on to live and work together primarily at Taliesin in Wisconsin, where she became a central organizer of his domestic life and helped support the apprenticeship community that grew up around his studio.

events.title: Launches the Taliesin Fellowship
events.description: In 1932, Wright and Olgivanna established the Taliesin Fellowship, formalizing a community of apprentices who learned through work, living, and study under Wrights direction at Taliesin in [[Spring Green|Spring Green, Wisconsin]]. Over the following years he regained national prominence through major commissionsincluding [[Fallingwater]]and expanded the Fellowships year-round rhythm by creating a winter base at Taliesin West near [[Scottsdale|Scottsdale, Arizona]].

Spring Green.explanation: Village in Wisconsin where Wrights Taliesin estate served as the original headquarters of the Taliesin Fellowship and its apprenticeship program.

Scottsdale.explanation: Arizona city near the site of Taliesin West, established as the Fellowships winter headquarters in the desert outside Phoenix.

Fallingwater.explanation: Wrights 1935 house design built over a waterfall in Pennsylvania, often cited as a defining example of his organic architecture.

events.title: Receives Guggenheim commission
events.description: Wright was commissioned in 1943 to design the [[Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum|Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum]] in New York, a project that occupied him through years of iterative design and controversy. It became a defining late-career platform for his ideas about movement through space and the choreography of a public interior.

locations.name_modern: New York City, New York, United States

images.caption: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum skylight, Manhattan

Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum.explanation: A modern art museum conceived as the home for Solomon R. Guggenheim’s non-objective art collection, developed under the direction of Hilla von Rebay; Wright’s design ultimately opened in 1959.

events.title: Dies at age 91
events.description: Wright died on April 9, 1959, after a seven-decade career that ranged from early Prairie School experimentation to large-scale late projects. At the end he remained engaged with design work and the [[Taliesin Fellowship|apprentice community]] he had built around his practice.

Taliesin Fellowship.explanation: Wrights apprenticeship program and communal living/working group centered at Taliesin and Taliesin West.
